article_text:
After buying Brad Pitt’s Plan B Entertainment in 2022 and Peter Chernin’s North Road earlier this year, Mediawan has enlisted another major Hollywood player, Reese Witherspoon ‘s Hello Sunshine .

As with its previous acquisitions which were financed partly through stock, Mediawan is bringing Witherspoon into its shareholder base, joining a stellar roster of talent and producers who have invested in the Paris-based group, including Pitt, Chernin and Plan B partners Dede Gardner and Jeremy Kleiner, as well as See-Saw’s Iain Canning and Emilie Sherman. The company also launched LuckyChap International, the London-based arm of Margot Robbie’s company, last November.

Related Stories

Asif Kapadia on Bringing the ‘Profound’ ‘7 Up’ Documentary Series to a Close After More Than 60 Years: 'It's a Dream Job'

Doc Stories Unveils 12th Annual Film Lineup (EXCLUSIVE)

“For our 10th anniversary today, we’re working with Brad Pitt, Margot Robbie and Reese Witherspoon — all three of whom are extremely creative and recognized as such — it defines the company’s DNA in terms of its independence, its commitment to talent and its creativity,” said Mediawan co-founder and chairman Pierre-Antoine Capton in an exclusive interview with Variety less than a day after unveiling the deal.

Mediawan also managed to pick up Hello Sunshine at a fraction of the $900 million valuation the company had when Blackstone-backed Candle Media acquired a majority stake in 2021.

Variety understands that Mediawan paid on the lower end of tens of millions of dollars, although Capton declined to disclose the exact figure or financial terms.

“I won’t confirm. The bottom line is that we acquired 100% of Hello Sunshine along with Reese and Mediawan, from Candle Media, and the money we’re investing is going toward development and content creation. It’s truly being invested in the company,” said Capton, who credited Chernin and Jesse Jacobs, former shareholders in Hello Sunshine, for bringing the opportunity to Mediawan.

The momentum has shifted in favor of European companies, as traditional Hollywood power players are under pressure to cut costs, streaming platforms are becoming pickier and U.S. indie producers are eager to work in Europe, where they can produce at lower costs and own IP. While Mediawan has made a name for itself in Hollywood in the last five years, another European giant with French roots, Banijay, which just merged with British powerhouse All3Media, is also looking to invest in the U.S. scripted market where it hasn’t yet broken through.

The acquisition of Hello Sunshine by Mediawan also illustrates how much the business has changed since the streaming boom that fueled Hello Sunshine’s previous valuation. Candle Media, founded by former Disney executives Kevin Mayer and Tom Staggs, had bet heavily on Witherspoon’s star power, social media presence and book club, but that model became more difficult to monetize in recent years.

On whether Hello Sunshine will fare better under Mediawan than it did under Candle, Capton pointed to the prestigious track record of Witherspoon’s company, notably “Big Little Lies,” “The Morning Show” and the Apple TV series “Lucky,” adapted from a Reese’s Book Club selection.

“They’ve really excelled creatively. That said, unfortunately, from time to time, there are investment deals with companies that may be perceived as financial strategies. That’s not the case for us,” said Capton, who worked on the deal alongside Mediawan CCO Elisabeth D’Arvieu and Guillaume Izabel, head of strategy and M&A. “With Reese, we’re really looking for creativity, independence and vision. That’s what interests us, so we don’t put financial pressure on it. It’s truly an editorial, artistic and creative addition that we’re seeking.”

Capton also said Mediawan intends to bring Reese’s Book Club internationally, including through potential productions in France and elsewhere in Europe.

“For all Mediawan producers — whether they’re Italian, German, British or Australian — access to all the IP that Reese can leverage through her book club is something very rare,” Capton said. “Yesterday, when we announced Reese and Hello Sunshine’s arrival at Mediawan, all our producers called us asking: ‘How can we work with them? How can we access the IP? How can we co-produce with them?’ There was a very strong desire from all our producers.”

“The goal isn’t for Reese to produce more herself, because she’s already produced a lot, but for this to also to fuel and create co-productions with our various producers. That’s what we’re hoping for,” he added.

Asked about the skepticism surrounding the Hello Sunshine deal, similar to the doubts raised when Mediawan acquired Plan B, Capton pointed to the latter’s recent hits.

“Plan B has produced ‘F1’ and ‘Adolescence’ last year. They’ve announced a pretty incredible lineup of series and films, so we’re very happy,” Capton said. “We had to trust each other, and it also took time to show what Mediawan was all about.”

Capton also sees further avenues for Mediawan to expand its footprint in the U.S. “We’re going to continue. Peter Chernin ’s arrival at the group has helped us become more ambitious, and with KKR’s support and the help of our local teams, we’re going to do something quite unique.”

While he declined to address rumors that Mediawan was one of the companies circling Lionsgate, he said, “In our model, the more we can distribute worldwide, the better off we’ll be. So, we’re looking at all possible opportunities.”

The French executive, who splits his time between Los Angeles and Paris, is also optimistic about the prospects for groups like Mediawan following the recent Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, even as Skydance prepares to make massive cuts.

“Skydance has committed to producing a certain number of films each year. I believe we have a company built on the creativity of our talent, and so, together, we’ll continue to develop and produce even more,” he said, pointing out that “Backrooms” (North Road), “Adolescence” (Plan B) and Florian Zeller’s “Bunker” (Blue Morning Pictures), starring Javier Bardem and Penelope Cruz, were made by producers who are part of Mediawan. He also revealed that the company will soon announce a major deal on vertical formats. “I’m convinced that these successes will only grow with our global consolidation,” Capton concluded.

article_text:
Born in New York in 1947, Stephen Shore is one of the photographers who made color a serious medium in American art. He was 14 when Edward Steichen bought three of his prints for the Museum of Modern Art, and still a teenager when he photographed daily life at Andy Warhol’s Factory. In 1971, the Metropolitan Museum of Art gave him a solo show, making him the first living photographer exhibited there since Alfred Stieglitz. The following year, he crossed the United States with a small 35mm camera for “American Surfaces,” a visual diary of diners, motel rooms, meals and strangers. He then switched to an 8×10 view camera for the road trips that became Uncommon Places (1982), a landmark of the New Color generation. Shore has directed the photography program at Bard College since 1982, and his book The Nature of Photographs remains a reference for students worldwide.

On the occasion of his retrospective “Véhiculaire & Vernaculaire,” which was held at the Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson in Paris in 2024, Stephen Shore took part in a public conversation with Quentin Bajac, director of the Jeu de Paume, held in the heart of the exhibition. Bajac knows the work closely: as chief curator of photography at the Museum of Modern Art, he organized Shore’s first career-spanning survey in the United States in 2017.

59 minutes, in English.

article_text:
The life and legacy of legendary Egyptian artist Mohamed Mounir is set to be explored in a biopic spearheaded by The Film Committee at Media City Qatar .

The Film Committee has acquired the rights to document Mounir’s life story, with partners on the project set to include a leading regional studio and other partners, which have yet to be unveiled.

The project was announced at the Film Committee’s Doha Industry Days, just hours after the Qatari body gave an update on previously announced biopic Caesar , about Syrian whistleblower Farid Al-Madhhan, announcing Taim Hasan as it star.

Steven Paul Talks Up Federal Film & TV Tax Credit: "It's Going To Be Good For The World" - Industry Days Doha

Mounir’s career spans nearly five decades across music, film and television.

Watch on Deadline

His 1981 breakthrough album ‘Shababeek’ established him as one of Egypt ’s most distinctive artists, with his work characterized by its fusion of Nubian folk and Arabic pop with Western genres like jazz, blues, and reggae.

He is known to his fans across the Middle East and beyond as “El King” in reference to his 1998 album and play ‘El Malek Howwa El Malek’ ((The King is The King).

Also working in cinema, his some 20 credits including collaborations with late Egyptian filmmaker Youssef Chahine on films including Egyptian Story (1982) and Destiny, which played in Out of Competition in Cannes in 1997 and was then selected as Egypt’s Oscar entry.

Mounir was born into a Nubian family in a village in Southern Egypt, where he spent his early childhood. His family moved to Cairo, after the village was resettled due to the construction of the Aswan Dam in the 1960s, where his singing voice was discovered when he sang at a family gathering.

The Film Committee said the biopic will trace Mounir’s journey from his humble beginnings to becoming one of the Arab world’s most celebrated and influential artists, revealing untold details, surprises, stories and anecdotes.

“Mohamed Mounir’s music holds a special place in the lives of audiences across Egypt and the Arab world,” said Film Committee at Media City Qatar Chair Hassan Al Thawadi.

“ Bringing his story to the big screen is an opportunity to celebrate his artistry, the cultural heritage his work represents and its lasting social relevance, a story that connects generations of fans across the region and has the power to resonate with audiences around the world,” he continued.

“This project also builds on our recent investment in extraordinary life stories from the region and reflects our ambition to develop a world-leading slate of biographical films that brings these stories to audiences globally.”

Alongside the feature film, plans include a behind-the-scenes documentary featuring interviews with Mounir and those who have lived and worked alongside him, as well as documenting the development and production of the biopic.

With development in the early stages, the hunt is now on for an actor to play Mounir.

article_text:
劇場版「進撃の巨人」前編 紅蓮の弓矢

劇場公開日： 2026年10月23日

解説・あらすじ

諫山創の人気コミックをアニメ化し、2013年4～9月に放送されて大ヒットを記録したテレビシリーズ「進撃の巨人」全25話を再編集した劇場版2部作の前編（テレビシリーズ第1～13話）。音声は新ダビングの5.1chリマスター、映像はブルーレイパッケージ用の修正版を使用し、テレビ版では未公開のシーンも含まれている。主題歌はテレビシリーズも担当して話題となったLinked Horizonによる新曲「紅蓮の座標」となり、エンディングテーマは劇伴も手がける澤野弘之が担当。 人を食らう謎の巨人に支配された世界で、人類は高さ50メートルの巨大な防壁を築き、その内側で暮らしていた。少年エレン・イェーガーは、まだ見ぬ外の世界を夢見ていたが、ある時、壁をも超える超大型巨人が出現し、その夢は打ち砕かれる。母親を目の前で巨人に食われてしまったエレンは、怒りを胸に、巨人と戦う訓練兵団へ入団する。 2026年10月にSCREEN X、4DX、ULTRA 4DXで再上映。

2014年製作／119分／G／日本 配給：ポニーキャニオン 劇場公開日：2026年10月23日

その他の公開日：2014年11月22日（日本初公開）

原則として東京で一週間以上の上映が行われた場合に掲載しています。 ※映画祭での上映や一部の特集、上映・特別上映、配給会社が主体ではない上映企画等で公開されたものなど掲載されない場合もあります。

title_original: Luciano Sozio tra i protagonisti della XXI Biennale Città di Penne con la mostra “Stati di Transizione”
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "XXI Biennale Città di Penne Stati di Transizione – Transitional States 31 ottobre – 29 novembre 2026 | Penne (PE)"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Cinque rassegne, quattro luoghi espositivi principali e un percorso tra arte contemporanea, sperimentazione e nuove possibilità di interpretazione. Dal 31 ottobre al 29 novembre 2026, la XXI Biennale Città di Penne presenta Stati di Transizione – Transitional States , un progetto espositivo articolato in cinque rassegne, distribuite in quattro spazi della Città e dedicate alle ricerche di artisti italiani e internazionali. Promossa dalla Fondazione Musei di Penne, dal Comune di Penne e dall’Accademia di Belle Arti dell’Aquila, con la collaborazione dalla Cooperativa Cogecstre e della Collezione Nato Frascà, la Biennale mette in relazione esperienze artistiche differenti attraverso un tema comune: la transizione, intesa come condizione di passaggio, apertura e trasformazione dei linguaggi. Il progetto assume l’incertezza non come limite, ma come possibilità critica e generativa. Le opere proposte non si esauriscono in dichiarazioni esplicite né ricercano necessariamente esiti formali definitivi: interrogano questioni estetiche, politiche, sociali e percettive, sollecitando il pubblico a costruire interpretazioni, riconoscere contraddizioni e immaginare significati ulteriori. Ne emerge una concezione dell’arte come spazio di ricerca e di confronto, capace di mettere in discussione le convenzioni e di aprire prospettive inedite. Il percorso coinvolge il Museo MaMEC, l’Auditorium San Giovanni Evangelista, alcuni ambienti dell’ex Tribunale e l’ex Convento del Carmine, intrecciando mostre internazionali, ricerche sui linguaggi contemporanei, approfondimenti storico-artistici e pratiche sperimentali delle nuove generazioni. L’evento di apertura si svolgerà il 31 ottobre alle 16.00 presso la Sala Consiliare, a seguire l’apertura di tutte le sedi espositive, per concludere il pomeriggio con un evento musicale a cura di Fornace del Bono ed Eco Brain, presso la sede dell’ex Convento del Carmine alle ore 20.00. L’orario di apertura delle mostre fino al 29 novembre, sarà il venerdì e il sabato ore 16:00/20:00 • domenica ore 10:00/13:00 16:00/20:00."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/11/01-Exhibition-view-XXI-Biennale-di-Penne-2026.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "01 Exhibition view XXI Biennale di Penne 2026", "credit": "Exibart"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "• MAMeC Museo d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea, Via Muzio Pansa 37"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "BRIDGING 2 a cura di Lorand Hegyi"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A cura di Lorand Hegyi, Bridging n. 2 prosegue il progetto pluriennale Bridging, nato nell’ambito dell’Aragno Humanities Forum per intensificare la collaborazione tra artisti italiani e internazionali e favorire relazioni dirette tra i protagonisti della cultura. Dopo la prima tappa dedicata a tre artisti italiani appartenenti a una generazione successiva alla Transavanguardia, questa seconda rassegna presenta in Italia le ricerche di Lois Weinberger, Hubert Scheibl e Alois Mosbacher, artisti austriaci accomunati da un approccio capace di mettere in relazione la sperimentazione formale con una più ampia riflessione culturale e sociologica. “Una mostra eccezionale, con artisti internazionali di straordinaria importanza, una proposta inedita in Italia. La prima occasione per la cultura artistica italiana di incontrare la ricerca di tre maestri fondamentali della cultura artista europea”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/11/02-Installation-view-2026-XXI-Biennale-di-Penne-.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "02 Installation view 2026 XXI Biennale di Penne", "credit": "Exibart"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "• Auditorium San Giovanni Evangelista, Largo San Giovanni Evangelista 121"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "STATI DI TRANSIZIONE – TRANSITIONAL STATES a cura di Antonio Zimarino e Angela Madesani"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "La mostra Stati di Transizione – Transitional States, a cura di Antonio Zimarino e Angela Madesani, riunisce artisti che affrontano l’opera d’arte non soltanto attraverso le sue qualità estetiche e stilistiche, ma interrogandone il senso, le modalità di percezione e le possibilità interpretative: arte intesa come spazio di possibilità. XXI Biennale Città di Penne Stati di Transizione – Transitional States 31 ottobre – 29 novembre 2026 | Penne (PE)

Cinque rassegne, quattro luoghi espositivi principali e un percorso tra arte contemporanea, sperimentazione e nuove possibilità di interpretazione. Dal 31 ottobre al 29 novembre 2026, la XXI Biennale Città di Penne presenta Stati di Transizione – Transitional States , un progetto espositivo articolato in cinque rassegne, distribuite in quattro spazi della Città e dedicate alle ricerche di artisti italiani e internazionali. Promossa dalla Fondazione Musei di Penne, dal Comune di Penne e dall’Accademia di Belle Arti dell’Aquila, con la collaborazione dalla Cooperativa Cogecstre e della Collezione Nato Frascà, la Biennale mette in relazione esperienze artistiche differenti attraverso un tema comune: la transizione, intesa come condizione di passaggio, apertura e trasformazione dei linguaggi. Il progetto assume l’incertezza non come limite, ma come possibilità critica e generativa. Le opere proposte non si esauriscono in dichiarazioni esplicite né ricercano necessariamente esiti formali definitivi: interrogano questioni estetiche, politiche, sociali e percettive, sollecitando il pubblico a costruire interpretazioni, riconoscere contraddizioni e immaginare significati ulteriori. Ne emerge una concezione dell’arte come spazio di ricerca e di confronto, capace di mettere in discussione le convenzioni e di aprire prospettive inedite. Il percorso coinvolge il Museo MaMEC, l’Auditorium San Giovanni Evangelista, alcuni ambienti dell’ex Tribunale e l’ex Convento del Carmine, intrecciando mostre internazionali, ricerche sui linguaggi contemporanei, approfondimenti storico-artistici e pratiche sperimentali delle nuove generazioni. L’evento di apertura si svolgerà il 31 ottobre alle 16.00 presso la Sala Consiliare, a seguire l’apertura di tutte le sedi espositive, per concludere il pomeriggio con un evento musicale a cura di Fornace del Bono ed Eco Brain, presso la sede dell’ex Convento del Carmine alle ore 20.00. L’orario di apertura delle mostre fino al 29 novembre, sarà il venerdì e il sabato ore 16:00/20:00 • domenica ore 10:00/13:00 16:00/20:00.

• MAMeC Museo d’Arte Moderna e Contemporanea, Via Muzio Pansa 37

BRIDGING 2 a cura di Lorand Hegyi

A cura di Lorand Hegyi, Bridging n. 2 prosegue il progetto pluriennale Bridging, nato nell’ambito dell’Aragno Humanities Forum per intensificare la collaborazione tra artisti italiani e internazionali e favorire relazioni dirette tra i protagonisti della cultura. Dopo la prima tappa dedicata a tre artisti italiani appartenenti a una generazione successiva alla Transavanguardia, questa seconda rassegna presenta in Italia le ricerche di Lois Weinberger, Hubert Scheibl e Alois Mosbacher, artisti austriaci accomunati da un approccio capace di mettere in relazione la sperimentazione formale con una più ampia riflessione culturale e sociologica. “Una mostra eccezionale, con artisti internazionali di straordinaria importanza, una proposta inedita in Italia. La prima occasione per la cultura artistica italiana di incontrare la ricerca di tre maestri fondamentali della cultura artista europea”

• Auditorium San Giovanni Evangelista, Largo San Giovanni Evangelista 121

STATI DI TRANSIZIONE – TRANSITIONAL STATES a cura di Antonio Zimarino e Angela Madesani

La mostra Stati di Transizione – Transitional States, a cura di Antonio Zimarino e Angela Madesani, riunisce artisti che affrontano l’opera d’arte non soltanto attraverso le sue qualità estetiche e stilistiche, ma interrogandone il senso, le modalità di percezione e le possibilità interpretative: arte intesa come spazio di possibilità. In esposizione le opere di Tina Bellini, Francesca Quintilio, Minus Log, Vanessa Di Lodovico, Ugo Giletta, Paolo Chiasera, Alberto Messina, Diego Soldà, Antonio Scaccabarozzi, Luciano Sozio, Marco Cordero, Elena Modorati e Irina Razumovskaya. Le ricerche presentate condividono l’attenzione per linguaggi che si sottraggono alla retorica e alle definizioni rigide. Le forme tradizionali vengono rilette, decostruite e ricomposte; la chiarezza apparente lascia spazio all’insolito, al dubbio, alla contraddizione e alla riduzione all’essenziale.

• Ex Tribunale, Salita Annunziata

SPAZI DI TRANSIZIONE Trame, storie, sogni, trasparenze a cura di Antonio Zimarino, Mario Costantini, Sibilla Panerai, Franca D’Angelo Percorsi e Apparizioni: Nato Frascà a Parigi nei primi anni ’60 a cura di Sibilla Panerai, Franca D’Angelo Negli ambienti dell’ex tribunale, la prima sezione a cura di Antonio Zimarino e Mario Costantini, mette a confronto le ricerche di Cristian Boffelli e Kaori Miyayama, due artisti che lavorano sul disegno e sulla stampa su tessuto, intrecciando riferimenti e sensibilità della tradizione orientale ed europea. La seconda sezione a cura di Sibilla Panerai, Antonio Zimarino, e Franca D’Angelo, presenta una selezione di opere su carta realizzate da Nato Frascà a Parigi tra il 1961 e il 1962, negli anni iniziali della sua ricerca artistica. L’esposizione si inserisce nel ventennale della scomparsa dell’artista, figura centrale della sperimentazione italiana del secondo Novecento e tra i fondatori del Gruppo Uno.

• Ex Convento del Carmine, Via Clemente de Caesaris

QUEL CHE RESTA È MIRAGGIO ACCADEMIA DI BELLE ARTI L’AQUILA a cura di Antonello Antico, Maurizio Coccia e Enzo De Leonibus

Completa il programma della Biennale Quel che resta è miraggio, mostra nata dalla Summer School 2026 dell’Accademia di Belle Arti dell’Aquila, a cura di Antonello Antico, Maurizio Coccia ed Enzo De Leonibus, con coordinamento di Maurizio Coccia e in collaborazione con Gianni Moretti. Svoltasi dal 28 settembre al 4 ottobre La mostra restituisce gli esiti di questo percorso attraverso un insieme eterogeneo di performance, installazioni e opere, espressione delle riflessioni delle nuove generazioni sul tema della transizione e sulle possibilità di sperimentare forme e linguaggi. Gli artisti partecipanti sono Adele Bianchi, Massimo Camplone, Alessandro Crescenzi, Francesco delle Monache, Paolo Di Battista, Valentina Equizi, Gemma Maria La Cecilia, Mattia Pio Mazza, Simone Mostaccioli, Ipek Ansi Ortakol, Giorgia Tatangelo, Alice Tonelli e Denis Tuncbilek.

article_text:
“Wildwood” director Travis Knight is weighing in on Hollywood’s use of AI.

“I’m not embracing it at all,” Knight told me Wednesday night at AFI Fest’s opening night U.S. premiere of “Wildwood.” “I see technology as a tool, and we use technology at Laika. A pencil is technology, a paintbrush is technology, a 3D printer is a computer is technology. Technology is useful when you put it in the hands of people, when you put it in the hands of artists who can amplify their voice.

“Technology is not useful when it takes the place of the artist, and that’s the concern with generative AI,” he continued. “It’s an amazing piece of technology, but the concern is that when it supplants the artist, then we have an issue because the computer cannot speak about humanity at all. “Wildwood” is a stop-motion fantasy feature about a young girl (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) who travels into a forbidden forest when her baby brother is kidnapped by a murder of crows. It took 16 years to complete the film, Knight said.

“Sixteen years is a long time,” Knight said. “As I’ve said before, this film is old enough to have driven me to the premiere tonight. But it’s a funny thing because it’s a big fantasy story. It’s a big sweeping adventure story. It’s a beautiful extravaganza. It’s an epic, but that’s not something that sustains you for 16 years.

He continued, “At the heart of it, it has to be something that means something to you and that’s the thing I’m most proud of is that underneath it all, it is something that is really heartfelt, it’s beautiful, it’s emotional and that’s the thing I hope audiences take away from this.”

Knight doesn’t believe that AI could have helped speed up the process — at least not if he wanted to maintain the highest quality. “That very notion fills me with rage,” he said. “Look, that’s the world we live in and the technology seems like it’s only pushing us in one direction, which is everything is going to be simpler. Everything is going to be automated; everything is going to be easier. What I would say to that is that there is something special about the human touch. There is something beautiful about humanity. And that’s one thing that stop motion represents. Stop-motion represents humanity at its finest creativity, emotion, care, devotion, time.

“That’s something that AI could never do because a computer has never felt anything,” Knight added. “It’s never felt loss or love or pain, and that’s something that people can feel and that’s something you feel in something that was made by people.”

The cast of “Wildwood” also includes Jacob Tremblay, Angela Bassett, Jake Johnson, Carey Mulligan, Maya Erskine, Mahershala Ali, Awkwafina, Amandla Stenberg and Tantoo Cardinal.

Bassett talked about recording her work during COVID. “I wanted to get out of the house, get creative again,” she told me. “It was just right on time.”

article_text:
On the occasion of Rêvalités , Galerie Anthony Roth is pleased to present the photographic work of Adam Akner for the first time. Through reconstructed landscapes, spaces traversed and human figures reduced to a few silhouettes, the artist creates images that lie on the boundary between reality and imagination.

Drawing on the world around him, the artist composes images in which reality seems to shift. Through montage and superimposition, spaces converge, perspectives become elusive and scales are disrupted. The landscapes remain familiar, yet something escapes their apparent clarity. A silhouette, a horizon line, a building or an open expanse become elements of a reconstructed reality in which several perceptions of the world can coexist.

It is within this in-between space that Adam Akner situates what he calls a “Rêvalité”: not a dream that replaces reality, but another way of inhabiting and observing it. Black and white removes colour to reveal the lines, shapes and relationships of light that structure the image. The viewer’s gaze moves beyond the photographed moment to linger on what remains uncertain.

The image thus seeks neither to document a place nor to impose a narrative. It becomes a territory to explore, leaving viewers free to project their own sensations, memories and questions onto it. The landscape takes on a mental dimension: the montage does not seek to create a fantastical world, but to shift reality just enough to reveal another way of perceiving it.

With Rêvalités , Adam Akner invites us not so much to recognise what we are looking at as to accept that we can no longer be entirely certain of it. Each photograph becomes an open fragment, somewhere between presence and absence, certainty and doubt, reality and imagination. As Jean-Pierre Mosca writes, “Meaning is never entirely given: it is constructed through the gaze of the viewer.”

In 2026, Rêvalités , an art book devoted to this photographic exploration, is published, with a foreword by Fernand Girard, President of the Société Académique Arts-Sciences-Lettres, and an introduction by Jean-Pierre Mosca, President of the Photography Section of the Salon des Artistes Français. A book signing will take place on Thursday, 12 November, during the exhibition opening.

Adam Akner

Born in 1960, Adam Akner has devoted himself fully to photography since 2021, following a thirty-five-year career as a Doctor of Pharmacy.

His work has notably been exhibited at the Grand Palais as part of Art Capital, at ArtExpo New York, and at the Salon d’Automne in Paris, where he was selected in 2023 and 2024. He has received several distinctions, including a Gold Medal at the Monochrome Photography Awards in 2023, the Grand Prix Photo de Saint-Tropez in 2024, and the Vermeil Medal of the Société Académique Arts-Sciences-Lettres in 2025.

article_text:
Zearo: It Follows Me Quietly Still

★★★★☆

Desire is a quiet, private, lonely thing in Malaysian painter Zearo’s world. In a single monumental image that spans almost the entire gallery, Zearo depicts men in a park at night, waiting, hoping, longing for companionship and love, but it feels like it might never come.

The park in the centre of the painting is a cruising spot, a place for men to express their sexuality in a society where that isn’t an acceptable thing to do. The men smoke languidly, leaning against trees, or lie impatiently on the grass. Some have found each other, they embrace or talk, but most are isolated, alone despite being in one of the only places where they don’t have to be.

The painting is called The Curfew. Read from left to right, it’s a journey from daytime through the early hours and on to dawn, when desire has to be hidden again. This is a painting of a window of opportunity – a chance to be free – that won’t stay open for long.

Upstairs, the paintings are smaller, depicting interior scenes in bedrooms and living rooms, but no less lonely and dreamlike. It seems to be perpetually dusk in Zearo’s world, like life is always on the precipice of transformation that never comes.

Zearo makes hazy, fuzzy, melancholy paintings filled with intricate details and symbolism. Like Salman Toor at the Courtauld and the recent Louis Fratino show at David Zwirner, queerness here is presented in elegiac, quiet, nostalgic ways, with this gentle 90s colour palette. It’s something permitted but barely accepted, suffused with loss and angst.

The Sunday Painter, London, until 19 December

Richie Culver: The Persistence of Things

★★★★☆

Richie Culver has encased history in resin, just like that mosquito preserved in amber in Jurassic Park. But this isn’t the ancient, prehistoric, geological past. This is personal memories, hazy nostalgia, the lost joys of youth preserved in thick, gloopy, oozing toxic plastic.

A pair of white Reeboks – signifiers of a youth spent at raves, every filthy scuff earned through hypnotic movement in some field or club long ago – is frozen in yellowed resin. Behind it, a cap has been pinned to a sheet of timber and framed against gluey, sticky cardboard, another marker of the past saved for the present.

But this is more than just rave-culture nostalgia, it’s Culver reckoning with what’s happened since those heady party days. Another Reebok has been bent and glued into a twisted, awkward shape. On its sole there’s now a photo of Culver’s stepfather in the final days before he died. Pictures of old clothes have been pasted on cardboard around the gallery, a sheet of wood is covered in staples and ripped fragments of images. On the wall, a mirror is grubby and opaque with glue, making your reflection opaque and fuzzy. It’s like Culver is trying to sift through the past, through what he was, trying to understand who he is now that it’s gone, but the answer is too out of focus to decipher.

I like Culver’s art, a lot. I want to see more of his post-rave minimalism, somewhere bigger. But shown here, in the basement of someone’s flat (you have to book an appointment via the website), the domesticity amps up the introspection, the queasy, uneasy nostalgia, the feeling that the past is a distant world that you will never ever be able to grasp again.

Pacheco, London, until 19 December

David Micheaud: Frequency Illusion

★★★★☆

When he was a student, David Micheaud got a job operating the Bournemouth Eye, a tethered hot air balloon tourist attraction that floats over the coastal city. They offered him the job full-time. He could see his life’s path laid out before him: four decades of balloon tethering, retirement, death.

He said no and became an artist instead, but that big old balloon seems to have haunted him ever since. There’s one in the middle of this small show, drooping bulbously from the ceiling. And the orb appears in every work on the wall – his first foray into pastels after a body of quiet, austere paintings. It’s a red buoy with a boat tethered to it, it’s a paper Ikea ceiling lamp, it’s the knob on top of a banister, a ball on a table. All these orbs are weird, ghostly presences – he draws precisely but foggily, everything is hazy, uncomfortable, all the shadows are harsh, all the lighting is dramatic. They’re awesome images, strange and discomfiting. It’s like he escaped a fate that just keeps coming back to pester him, leaving the traces of what could have been dotted throughout his life for him to notice.

In one image, a huge orb has crushed a man, based on a still from 60s TV show The Prisoner. Life can crush you, or you can dodge the ball of fate and make your own way.

Xxijra Hii, London, until 5 December

Amélie Mckee: Solarium

★★★★☆

The phrase “green energy” promises natural, ecological optimism. But it’s something a lot more toxic in Amélie Mckee’s debut UK exhibition, a few doors down from David Micheaud’s show.

Two ionic columns in the centre of the space have been turned into Tesla towers, most of the stone replaced with metal. In the middle of each, vintage 1930s dinner plates glow a sickly green because they’re made of uranium. The same stuff we use to build nuclear weapons used to be fine china for dinner parties. Mckee is making the line between caloric energy and industrial power feel pretty blurry.

On a plinth, more gross glow: a can of Monster Energy drink has been poured into a 1928 pin tray with the figure of a nude woman now seeming to swim in the yellow sludge.

The gallery text is some of the most incomprehensible semi-English bullshit I’ve read for a long while, which makes figuring the work out a little tricky, but I think I get it. This is about authority and energy, about fuel on an industrial and personal level, about how toxic our relationship with power (who controls it, who consumes it, the greed and evil of it all) has become. It’s all framed in a semi-retro, toxic sludge aesthetic. Power corrupts, but energy is monstrous.

Plicnik Space Initiative, London, until 19 December

Dazu werden die Dokumente mit einem digitalen Fingerabdruck mit Verschlüsselungstechnik, einem Zeitstempel sowie einer institutionellen Signatur versehen."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Besuch bei Google"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Weimer, der sich in dieser Woche zu Gesprächen mit Vertretern großer US-Technologieunternehmen wie Google und YouTube in den USA aufhielt, betonte die Bedeutung des Projekts: Der Erhalt des kollektiven Gedächtnisses und der Schutz historischer Wahrheiten seien fundamentale Säulen einer wehrhaften Demokratie. KI kann historische Dokumente täuschend echt verändern – und echte Quellen als Fälschungen erscheinen lassen. Wie ein neues Projekt Archive und Gedenkstätten schützen soll

Kulturstaatsminister Wolfram Weimer und Google.org – die gemeinnützige Stiftung des Technologiekonzerns Google – unterstützen gemeinsam ein Projekt gegen die Fälschung von historischen Ausstellungsstücken. Mit der "Global Authentic Memory Initiative" (GAMI) sollen historische Digitalbestände in Archiven, Museen und Gedenkstätten wirksam vor Fälschungen durch generative Künstliche Intelligenz geschützt werden.

Das Bundeskulturministerium stellt für das Projekt Fördermittel in Höhe von 100.000 Euro bereit, weitere 300.000 Euro steuert Google.org bei. GAMI bietet eine herstellerunabhängige und offene technische Lösung an, mit der sich die Echtheit historischer Dokumente digital nachweisen lässt. Dazu werden die Dokumente mit einem digitalen Fingerabdruck mit Verschlüsselungstechnik, einem Zeitstempel sowie einer institutionellen Signatur versehen.

Besuch bei Google

Weimer, der sich in dieser Woche zu Gesprächen mit Vertretern großer US-Technologieunternehmen wie Google und YouTube in den USA aufhielt, betonte die Bedeutung des Projekts: Der Erhalt des kollektiven Gedächtnisses und der Schutz historischer Wahrheiten seien fundamentale Säulen einer wehrhaften Demokratie. Man nehme die Sorgen von Gedenkstätten ernst und schütze wertvolle Archivbestände im digitalen Zeitalter dauerhaft.

Hintergrund der Initiative ist ein Hilferuf von NS-Gedenkstätten in einem offenen Brief vom 13. Januar 2026. Darin warnten die Einrichtungen vor der Gefahr der sogenannten "Lügner-Dividende": Durch den Vormarsch generativer KI bestehe das Risiko, dass echte historische Dokumente fälschlicherweise als KI-Generat abgetan oder synthetische Fälschungen als Tatsachen verbreitet werden. Im Gegensatz zu modernen Medien enthalten historische Objekte meist keine eingebetteten Herkunftsnachweise.

Projekt aus Bayern

GAMI ist ein Projekt des bayerischen Startups Authentic Memory gUG, einer Ausgründung der Technischen Universität München und der Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München unter Leitung von Gründer Pablo Toussaint. Erste erfolgreiche Testläufe des Verfahrens gab es bereits mit den KZ-Gedenkstätten Dachau und Flossenbürg.

Ungeachtet der Zusammenarbeit dringt Kulturstaatsminister Weimer weiterhin auf eine regulatorische Verschärfung gegenüber großen Tech-Konzernen: Er plant eine Digitalabgabe für Plattformen wie Google und Meta, um mit den Einnahmen die heimische Medien- und Kulturlandschaft sowie den Lokaljournalismus zu stärken.
